header: IN THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH,
Abdul Moiz Jafri, Advocate, for the Petitioners.
Mehreen Ibrahim, DAG, for the Federation of Pakistan.
Iftikhar Ahmed, Advocate, for the National Tariff Commission.
body: YOUSUF ALI SAYEED, J. - The Petitioner No. 1, an association of iron and steel merchants registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (the “SRA”), and the Petitioner No. 2, its Joint Secretary, have invoked the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution so as to impugn their exclusion from Anti-Dumping Investigation No. ADC No. 73/2026/NTC/CCCS (the "Investigation") being conducted by the National Tariff Commission (the "Commission") under the Anti-Dumping Duties Act, 2015 (the "ADDA") in respect of alleged dumped imports of Colour Coated Cold Rolled Steel Coils/Sheets originating in and/or exported from the People's Republic of China.

2. The Petitioners assert that, in the context of the Investigation, they fall within the definition of an "interested party" under Section 2(j) of the ADDA, and have impugned a letter dated 21.05.2026 whereby the request of the Petitioner No.1 to be registered in that capacity was declined by the Commission (the "Impugned Decision"), whilst also seeking a direction that the Petitioner No.1 be so registered and afforded the incidents of that status.
3. The facts giving rise to the Petition are largely a matter of record and are not seriously in dispute, which may be summarised as follows:

(a) On an application dated 16.03.2026 submitted under Sections 20 and 24 of the ADDA read with Rule 3 of the Anti-Dumping Duties Rules, 2022 (the "Rules") by M/s International Steels Limited, Karachi, the Commission initiated the Investigation under Section 23 of the ADDA through a Notice of Initiation dated 25.04.2026 (the “Notice”).

(b) The Notice called upon interested parties, as defined in Section 2(j), to identify themselves within ten days of its publication, by furnishing their name, line of business, authorized person and contact particulars, and invited their views, comments and evidence within forty-five days. It also announced that a public file had been established under Rule 7 of the Rules, available to interested parties for review and copying.

(c) The Petitioners assert that the Notice, though dated 25.04.2026, was uploaded on the Commission's website only on 28.04.2026, and that the Petitioner No. 1 sought registration the very next day (i.e. on 29.04.2026), followed by reminders dated 07.05.2026, 13.05.2026, 15.05.2026 and 18.05.2026.

(d) Through the Impugned Decision, the Commission informed the Petitioner No. 1 that since it was not registered with the Directorate General of Trade Organizations ("DGTO") and Section 5(3) of the Trade Organizations Act, 2013 (the “TOA”) prohibited the use of the word "Association" by an unregistered trade organization, it could not be registered as an interested party, while observing that individual importers were eligible to participate and submit their views independently.

(e) The Petitioners also set out a history of having been registered as an interested party in several earlier investigations and reviews concerning flat-rolled steel products, including ADC No. 51/2017/NTC/CCCS relating to the same product, and of having been refused registration in two more recent proceedings, i.e. ADC No. 35/2025/NTC/CRC/CV and the Second Sunset Review in ADC No. 35/2015/NTC/CRC, on the same ground of nonregistration with DGTO.

4. The Commission filed its para-wise comments, wherein it stated inter alia that it had registered one association, namely the Pakistan Iron & Steel Merchants Association ("PISMA"), as well as the China Chamber of Commerce of Metals, Minerals & Chemicals Importers & Exporters, 14 importers and 6 exporters as interested parties in the Investigation.
5. For purposes of the matter at hand, it merits consideration that Section 2(j) of the ADDA reads as follows:
"(j) "interested party" includes— (i) any exporter or foreign producer of an investigated product;
(ii) any importer of an investigated product; (iii) trade or business association a majority of the members of which are producers, exporters or importers of an investigated product;
(iv) the government of an exporting country;
(v) any producer of a domestic like product in Pakistan;

(vi) trade or business associations a majority of the members of which produce a domestic like product in Pakistan; and (vii) such other person or group of persons as the Commission may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify;"

6. Turning to the TOA, sub-section (3) of Section 1 thereof provides that "It shall apply to trade organizations whose objects and business are not confined to a province", whereas clause (r) of Section 2 defines a "trade organisation" as follows:
"(r) "trade organisation" means an organisation which.- (i) is capable of being formed as a limited company within the meaning of the Ordinance;
(ii) is formed or intended to be formed with the object of promoting any trade, industry or service or any combination thereof;
(iii) prohibits payment of any profits to its members; and (iv) applies its income and profits for achieving its objects."
7. Section 5(3), on which the Impugned Decision rests, reads as follows:

"(3) No trade organisation other than a licensed and registered trade organisation shall use in its name or title the word "Federation" or "Chamber" or "Association" except an existing trade organisation which has applied for grant of licence under this Act: Provided that nothing in sub-section (3) shall apply to a company, association or body of persons formed for promoting art, science, religion, charity, sports, any profession other than trade, commerce, industry, service or any other subject which the Government may, by notification in the official gazette specify in this behalf."

8. Learned counsel for the Petitioners submitted that Section 2(j)(iii) of the ADDA was self-contained and required no more than that the association be a trade or business association a majority of whose members were producers, exporters or importers of the investigated product. Nothing in the ADDA or the Rules made a licence under the TOA a condition of that status, and the Commission could not read into the statute a requirement that the Legislature had not enacted. Reliance was placed in that regard on Tasneem Enterprises (Private) Limited v. National Tariff Commission and others (C.P. No. D-4561 of 2024, decided on 28.01.2025) as recognising the participatory framework that the ADDA affords to interested parties. He argued that in any event, the TOA bore no application to the Petitioner No. 1 by virtue of Section 1(3) thereof, as its objects and business were confined to the Province of Sindh, so that neither the licensing requirement nor Section 5(3) of that enactment could be invoked against it. He submitted that the Commission had registered the Petitioner No. 1 as an interested party in numerous earlier investigations, including one relating to the very same product, and its abrupt departure from that course without any change in the law was arbitrary and discriminatory, offending Articles 4, 10A, 18 and 25 of the Constitution. He submitted that the ADDA did not provide any remedy against a refusal of registration during the pendency of an investigation, and any remedy after its conclusion would be illusory, as the prejudice flowing from exclusion at the stage of submissions was irreversible.

9. Conversely, learned counsel for the Commission contended that the ADDA was a trade remedy law, and a "trade or business association" within the meaning of Section 2(j)(iii) of the ADDA necessarily denoted an association representing the trade or commercial interests of its members, which, it was said, had to be licensed under the TOA by the DGTO. He argued that the Petitioner No.1 did not qualify as an interested party as the DGTO had confirmed that it was unlicensed through letter F.No.18(61)/2008-TO dated 24.06.2025, in response to the Commission's query of 23.06.2025. He submitted further that the ADDA and the TOA had to be read together as part of a single coherent scheme, and as the latter enactment was in the field when the ADDA was passed, the reference in Section 2(j)(iii) to a trade or business association could only be to a "trade organisation" licensed and registered under the TOA, within the meaning of Section 2(r) thereof. He argued that the Petitioner No. 1 was a society registered under the SRA, which, by its Preamble and Section 20, catered only to charitable, literary, scientific and like objects, and not to the representation of commercial interests, hence it could not represent its members in the Investigation. He pointed out that Section 3 of the TOA, contained a non obstante provision, and argued that it overrode the laws relating to the registration of societies, so that every trade or business association had necessarily to be licensed under it. He submitted that the earlier registrations of the Petitioner No.1 by the Commission had proceeded on incomplete knowledge of the Petitioner No. 1's legal status, and could confer no perpetual right, with the refusal in the present case representing a "course correction" rather than a departure. He argued that the Petition was in any event superfluous, as the members of the Petitioner No.1 who imported the investigated product were free to seek registration individually under Section 2(j)(ii). Moreover, the interests of importers were already represented through PISMA, which had been registered, and had authorized the same representative as the Petitioner No. 1. Lastly, he submitted a petition under Article 199 would lie only to enforce a right that existed in law, not to create one, and by claiming to represent commercial interests, the Petitioner No. 1 was going beyond Section 20 of the SRA. He argued that the Petition was also not maintainable for that reason.

10. We have heard the arguments advanced and examined the record with the assistance of counsel. The test to be applied in determining the propriety of the Impugned Decision from a legal standpoint is well recognised. In Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223, Lord Greene M.R. explained that a person entrusted with a discretion "must, so to speak, direct himself properly in law. He must call his own attention to the matters which he is bound to consider. He must exclude from his consideration matters which are irrelevant to what he has to consider." Summarising the principle, it was held that the Court "is entitled to investigate the action of the local authority with a view to seeing whether they have taken into account matters which they ought not to take into account, or, conversely, have refused to take into account or neglected to take into account matters which they ought to take into account", and that, even where that question is answered in the authority's favour, the Court may still interfere if the authority has "come to a conclusion so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it". However, it was observed that the Court does so "not as an appellate authority to override a decision of the local authority, but as a judicial authority which is concerned, and concerned only, to see whether the local authority have contravened the law by acting in excess of the powers which Parliament has confided in them". These principles were later distilled by Lord Diplock in Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374, who classified the grounds of judicial review under three heads, "illegality", "irrationality" and "procedural impropriety". As to the first, it was said that "By 'illegality' as a ground for judicial review I mean that the decisionmaker must understand correctly the law that regulates his decision-making power and must give effect to it. Whether he has or not is par excellence a justiciable question to be decided, in the event of dispute, by those persons, the judges, by whom the judicial power of the state is exercisable." As to the second, irrationality was described as "what can by now be succinctly referred to as 'Wednesbury unreasonableness'", applying "to a decision which is so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question to be decided could have arrived at it". That formulation has been endorsed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Dr. Akhtar Hassan Khan and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others, 2012 SCMR 455, where, drawing upon Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) 6 SCC 651, it was observed that "the grounds upon which an administrative action is subject to control by judicial review can be classified as under:-- (i) Illegality: This means the decision-maker must understand correctly the law that regulates his decision-making power and must give effect to it. (ii) Irrationality, namely, Wednesbury unreasonableness. (iii) Procedural impropriety." It was also noted there that the concern of the Court is not whether a particular decision is fair, but "the manner in which those decisions have been taken". The present case, turning as it does on whether the Commission correctly understood the law regulating its power under Section 2(j)(iii), falls squarely within the first of those heads.

11. A related principle that must also be kept in view is that the legality of an order passed by a public functionary is to be judged by the reasons stated in the order itself, and cannot be supplemented or improved upon through fresh reasons offered in the comments or arguments subsequently advanced in its defence. The principle was succinctly stated by the Supreme Court of India in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner AIR 1978 SC 851, in the following terms:

"when a statutory functionary makes an order based on certain grounds, its validity must be judged by the reasons so mentioned and cannot be supplemented by fresh reasons in the shape of affidavit or otherwise. Otherwise, an order bad in the beginning may, by the time it comes to court on account of a challenge, get validated by additional grounds later brought out. We may here draw attention to the observations of Bose J. in Gordhandas Bhanji: 'Public orders, publicly made, in exercise of a statutory authority cannot be construed in the light of explanations subsequently given by the officer making the order of what he meant, or of what was in his mind, or what he intended to do. Public orders made by public authorities are meant to have public effect and are intended to effect the actings and conduct of those to whom they are addressed and must be construed objectively with reference to the language used in the order itself.'"

Though not binding upon us, that statement of the law commends itself as sound, and is apposite here, for while the Impugned Decision rests solely on the non-registration of the Petitioner No. 1 with the DGTO and the bar contained in Section 5(3) of the TOA, the comments of the Commission and argument advanced seek to sustain it on the additional ground of the Petitioner No. 1's registration under the SRA. We will return to that aspect in due course.

12. Turning firstly to the objection that the Petition is not maintainable because the Petitioner No. 1 lacks the capacity to represent the commercial interests of its members, it merits consideration that the objection relates to the very question that falls for determination and cannot be decided preliminarily. No objection was raised as to the availability of any alternate remedy under the ADDA itself, and rightly so, as Section 70(1) confers a right of appeal only on an "interested party", and only against the orders enumerated therein, which do not include a refusal to register a person as such. More fundamentally, a person who has been refused that status would not be in a position to invoke a remedy available only to those who enjoy it. Indeed, in Tasneem Enterprises (Supra), the adequate remedy of an interested party was held to lie in participation in an investigation, which is what the Impugned Decision denies to the Petitioners. Nor are we persuaded that the Petition is superfluous as the members of the Petitioner No. 1 who import the investigated product may seek registration individually under Section 2(j)(ii), or that PISMA has already been registered. Section 2(j) recognises importers and trade or business associations as distinct categories of interested party, and the availability of one does not detract from the other. If a person falls within clause (iii), the fact that its members might qualify in their own right under clause (ii) cannot be a reason in support of it being denied the status that the statute confers. Equally, the registration of a different association can have no bearing on the entitlement of the Petitioner No.1. Moreover, the Impugned Decision itself records that "individual importers are eligible to participate in the subject investigation and may submit their views, comments, or relevant information independently", and the comments go further, acknowledging that those members of the Petitioner No. 1 "who are importers of the investigated product" may join the Investigation in their individual capacity. In confining the association to participation through its members, the Commission has, in effect, substituted clause (ii) of Section 2(j) of the ADDA for clause (iii) thereof, and thereby read the latter out of the statute.

13. Moving on to the merits, the first question that warrants consideration is whether Section 2(j)(iii) contemplates only an association of a particular legal status, whether by virtue of licensing as a trade organisation or otherwise. In our view, it does not, for the reason that the same brings within the fold of an "interested party" a "trade or business association a majority of the members of which are producers, exporters or importers of an investigated product". The word "association" is not defined in the ADDA, and must therefore be given its ordinary meaning, which connotes a body of persons who have come together for a common purpose. The only qualification attached is that a majority of the members be producers, exporters or importers of the investigated product. The criterion thus turns on the composition of the membership, and says nothing about the statute under which the association is constituted, or whether it is licensed or registered. Furthermore, the definition is inclusive in its terms, with clause (vii) empowering the Commission to enlarge the class of interested parties by notification, and not to curtail it. It was urged on behalf of the Commission that the TOA and ADDA are in pari materia, and that, as the former enactment was already in the field when the latter was passed, the expression "trade or business association" can only refer to a "trade organisation" licensed under it. We are unable to agree, for statutes are said to be in pari materia when they deal with the same subject or form part of the same scheme, whereas the TOA regulates the licensing, registration and governance of chambers and associations of trade and industry, and the ADDA is a trade remedy statute governing the conduct of antidumping investigations. As such, the two do not share a subject. Even if they were to be read together, the argument would fail on its own terms. Furthermore, while promulgating the ADDA, the Legislature, with the TOA before it, chose not to employ the defined expression "trade organisation", or to refer to licensing under that enactment, but used the different and broader expression "trade or business association". Had the Legislature intended to confine Section 2(J)(iii) of the ADDA to licensed trade organisations, nothing would have been easier than to say so. Additionally, considering Section 1(3) of the TOA, which places provincially confined bodies outside that scheme altogether, it would be anomalous to hold that a body which the TOA does not regulate is for that very reason barred under the ADDA. That is not to say that the Commission must accept at face value every claim to be such an association, as it may legitimately call for material to satisfy itself that the association genuinely exists, as to the composition of its membership, and as to the authority of the person acting on its behalf. That is an inquiry into whether the criterion in clause (iii) is met and is quite distinct from imposing a qualification as to legal status that the clause does not contain. As things stand, the Impugned Decision did not address the criterion set out in clause (iii) at all. It did not record any finding as to whether a majority of the members of the Petitioner No.1 were importers of the investigated product, but proceeded solely on the basis that the Petitioner No. 1 was not registered with the DGTO, and that Section 5(3) of the TOA prohibited an unregistered trade organisation from using the word "Association" in its name. Even the reference to the National Tariff Commission Act, 2015 in the Impugned Decision is misplaced, as the relevant statue is the ADDA.

14. As for the contention that the registration of the Petitioner No. 1 under the SRA transgresses that enactment, as it does not extend to an association formed to advance business or commercial interests, the same is untenable for several reasons. Firstly, it forms no part of the Impugned Decision and, as discussed herein above, cannot be pressed into service to sustain it. Secondly, whether the Petitioner No.1 was properly granted registration under the SRA is a matter for a forum competent under that enactment, and so long as the registration subsists, the Commission has no jurisdiction to treat it as void or to sit in judgment over it for purposes of an investigation being conducted under the ADDA. Thirdly, the contention is in any event beside the point, for as held above, clause (iii) of Section 2(j) looks to the composition of an association's membership, not to its legal status, hence, even if the registration were found wanting, the Petitioner No.1 would not thereby cease to be an association a majority of whose members are importers of the investigated product, if that is otherwise shown to be so. Equally, the contention that Article 199 cannot be invoked to create a non-existent right is of no avail, as the right asserted is the statutory status conferred by Section 2(j)(iii), which exists if the criterion of that clause is met.

15. It is also not disputed that the Petitioner No. 1 was registered as an interested party in a series of earlier investigations and reviews, including ADC No. 51/2017/NTC/CCCS, which related to the same product. The Commission seeks to explain its change of stance as a "course correction" made upon gaining "full knowledge" of the Petitioner No. 1's legal status. However, the DGTO letter of 24.06.2025 on which the Commission itself relies shows that it was aware of the Petitioner No.1's unlicensed status by June 2025. Even so, the Petitioner No. 1 is shown to have participated in ADC No.

37/2015/NTC/GC/Circum/2024, in which the final determination was made on 27.06.2025. While a statutory authority is not bound in perpetuity by an erroneous view, a departure from a settled course must rest on a lawful basis, and here it does not, with the point being further underscored by the Commission's own stance, inasmuch having accepted that the members of the Petitioner No. 1 who import the investigated product are entitled to participate individually, and having raised no objection to their commercial interests being represented, the Commission offers no reason grounded in the ADDA as to why those same members should be denied a collective voice through the association to which they belong. Clause (iii) exists precisely to afford such a voice, and its utility is evident, for it enables traders who may lack the means to participate singly to do so collectively. Nor is that voice supplied by the registration of PISMA, a different association, through which the members of the Petitioner No. 1 have not chosen to be represented. The exclusion thus turns on nothing more than the licensing status of the association, a consideration that, as we have found, has no bearing on the criterion that the ADDA prescribes. A decision that permits the members to be heard singly, while barring them from being heard together on a ground the statute does not recognise, does not, in our view, admit of any rational justification.

16. As such, we are of the view that the Impugned Decision is unsustainable in law, having been founded on considerations extraneous to Section 2(j)(iii) of the ADDA while ignoring the criterion that the provision actually prescribes.

17. The Petition is accordingly allowed, and the Impugned Decision is set aside, with the request of the Petitioner No. 1 for registration as an interested party in the Investigation being deemed to be pending before the Commission. The Commission is directed to decide that request afresh within ten days of receipt of this judgment, by way of a speaking order, after affording the Petitioner No. 1 an opportunity to place material before it as to the composition of its membership. The request is to be decided strictly with reference to the criterion laid down in Section 2(j)(iii) of the ADDA, and without regard to the registration or otherwise of the Petitioner No. 1 under the TOA. Should the Petitioner No. 1 be registered, it shall be entitled to all the incidents of that status from the stage at which the Investigation then stands, including access to the public file, and due consideration shall be given to its submissions.
JUDGE JUDGE
